ACCEPTThe half-area theorem is correct under the exact stated hypotheses, and the written proof in (2)–(9) establishes it. The four binary pocket cases are valid; the actual matching implies the stated two-site capacity; and the pocket and bottom-boundary holes are disjoint physical sites.This is a scoped result: endpoints and matching edges may vary across the whole board, while the restrictions on black selections, occupied anchors, and the two bottom white sites remain essential hypotheses of this proof. It is not a universal grid bound.I base this verdict on the written mathematics. Omitting the additional forced hole  $(5,4)$  is a valid weakening. $g=(5,1)$  $x,r,s$  $2g\le x+r+s$ . $h=(5,3)$  $q,s,(5,4)$ At least two neighbours must be empty, so at least one of  $q,s$  is empty:  $h\le q+s$ .In particular, the treatment of  $(5,4)$  is sound. The proof deliberately does not include it among the nine pocket holes. Dropping a necessary emptiness condition weakens the local hypotheses; it does not invalidate the resulting implication.The anchors need only be occupied. Their being selected or matching endpoints makes no difference to these deductions.2. Actual matching implies the two-site Hall capacityLet  $A$  be the occupied sites among
$$r_{\rm site}=(5,0),\qquad s_{\rm site}=(5,2).$$
Because  $r,s$  denote emptiness indicators,
$$|A|=2-r-s.$$
The explicit hypothesis that these two sites are not selected is crucial: every member of  $A$  must therefore be an endpoint of the actual matching.Their complete board-neighbour sets are
$$N(r_{\rm site})=\{d_{\rm site},g_{\rm site}\},
\qquad
N(s_{\rm site})=\{e_{\rm site},g_{\rm site},h_{\rm site}\}.$$
Thus their union consists of precisely four distinct sites:
$$\{d_{\rm site},e_{\rm site},g_{\rm site},h_{\rm site}\}.$$
The actual mates of the members of  $A$ :lie in this union;are distinct, because  $M$  is a matching;are not selected, because  $T\cap P=\varnothing$ .Writing  $D=d+e+g+h$ , there are  $4-D$  unselected sites in that union. Consequently
$$2-r-s\le 4-D,$$
which rearranges to
$$D\le 2+r+s.$$
This proves (4).The capacity is necessary, not sufficient, for an actual matching. Some of the  $4-D$  unselected sites could be empty, and singleton neighbourhood restrictions can be stronger than this union bound. That causes no gap: the pocket lemma is proved for a relaxation that contains every actual feasible configuration.There is also no double use of a matching “payment” here. Equation (4) restricts which binary patterns are possible; it does not contribute an additional hole or a separately spendable surplus.3. D=d+e+g+h,\qquad
k=v+x+Q.$$

hold.If  $C=1$ , then  $Q\ge3$ , so either indicated triple contains at least two blanks, enough to dominate  $C+f\le2$ . If  $C=0$ , then  $C+f=f\le z$ , and  $z$  belongs to both triples.For (7), let  $E$  be binary with  $E\le w+q$ . Then

because  $q=1$ .Thus the final case is valid as written. Restoring  $a\le u$  proves the pocket lemma.4. The global compensation uses disjoint coordinatesEvery allowed black selection outside the eight-site pocket is
$$t_k=(5,k),\qquad k\text{ odd},\quad 5\le k\le c.$$
Its upper neighbour  $(4,k)$  is occupied by hypothesis. If  $t_k$  is selected, its left neighbour
$$\ell_k=(5,k-1)$$
must therefore be empty.The map  $t_k\mapsto\ell_k$  is injective, and its image lies in
$$L=\{(5,4),(5,6),\ldots,(5,c-1)\}.$$
The pocket’s only row-5 white sites are  $(5,0)$  and  $(5,2)$ . Its other white sites lie in rows 1–4. Therefore its nine white coordinates are disjoint from  $L$ .The black selections are partitioned just as cleanly: the pocket includes bottom black sites at columns  $1,3$ , while the tail begins at column  $5$ . Thus
$$|T_{\rm black}|
=
|T_{\rm black,pocket}|+|T_{\rm black,tail}|
\le
|H_{\rm white}\cap\text{pocket}|+|H_{\rm white}\cap L|
\le |H_{\rm white}|.$$
This is a valid addition of two cardinality inequalities over disjoint sets. No assumption of a local one-to-one assignment inside the pocket is needed: the pocket lemma already proves its joint cardinality bound.The boundary case  $c=5$  also works. There is one tail selection position,  $(5,5)$ , paid by  $(5,4)$ . At the rightmost site  $t_c$ , the proof uses the existing left neighbour and never requires a right neighbour outside the board.5. The half-area identity and specialization to the original class are exactEvery nearest-neighbour edge joins opposite colours, so an actual matching has
$$|P_{\rm white}|=|P_{\rm black}|=|M|.$$
Because  $T$  and  $P$  are disjoint,
$$J=|T|+|M|
=|T_{\rm black}|+|T_{\rm white}|+|P_{\rm white}|
=|T_{\rm black}|+|O_{\rm white}|.$$
There are exactly  $3(c+1)$  white sites on the six-row board. Hence
$$3(c+1)-J
=|H_{\rm white}|-|T_{\rm black}|
\ge0.$$
This establishes the claimed whole-board upper bound. No old matching edge, freezing property, or local colour-balance assumption enters this argument.6. Sharpness does not require accepting the claimed earlier constructionsUnder the exact stated hypotheses,  $T=\varnothing$  is permitted. Take

\bigcup_{k=0}^{c}
\left\{
\{(0,k),(1,k)\},
\{(2,k),(3,k)\},
\{(4,k),(5,k)\}
\right\}.$$
This is a perfect matching of the board. It has
$$P=R\supseteq P_0,\qquad T\subseteq T_0,$$
and the selected-degree condition is vacuous. Consequently
$$J=|M|=3(c+1).$$
So the exact maximum in the stated class follows without importing any claim about frozen or mixed attainers.The displayed nonempty  $T_0,P_0$  construction can also be checked directly. Set

\qquad

It does not independently establish the separate “complete freezing” assertion or the assertion about every previously studied mixed expansion, neither of which is needed for this theorem.7. Counterexamples: the degree-only statement fails, but the theorem does notThe note’s degree-only counterexample is correct. Its assignment satisfies (3), has six pocket selections and five pocket holes, and violates (4):
$$d+e+g+h=4>3=2+r+s.$$
Its occupied  $s=(5,2)$  has all three neighbours  $e,g,h$  selected, so it cannot have an actual matching mate. It is not a feasible counterexample to the theorem.There is also a useful example showing why two-site capacity can matter even when each singleton has a possible unselected mate. Take
$$a=g=0,\qquad b=C=d=e=f=h=1,$$
and
$$(u,v,w,x,y,z,q,r,s)
=(0,1,1,1,0,1,1,0,0).$$
All of (3) hold, again with six selections and five holes. Both  $r$  and  $s$  are occupied. Each has  $g$  as its only unselected potential mate: $r$  has neighbours  $d,g$ , with  $d$  selected. $s$  has neighbours  $e,g,h$ , with  $e,h$  selected.Thus singleton availability holds, but the two sites cannot receive distinct mates. Equation (4) detects this:
$$D=3>2=2+r+s.$$
These examples support the distinction made in the note: degree constraints alone are insufficient for the pocket inequality; actual matching supplies an additional necessary restriction.8. Equality, ancillary claims, and the limit of this acceptanceEquation (10) is valid with the intended definitions:  $H_{\rm pocket}$ ,  $H_L$ , and  $H_{\rm other}$  count white empty sites, while  $T_{\rm pocket}$  and  $T_{\rm tail}$  count the corresponding black selections. The first two differences are nonnegative by the pocket and tail bounds, and the final term is a cardinality. Equality is therefore equivalent to all three terms vanishing.Defining those shorthand quantities explicitly would improve clarity, especially  $H_{\rm other}$ ; this is not a defect in the proof.The tile paragraph is also correct at its stated global level:
$$\sum_{\rm tiles}\chi
=|R|-2|T|-|P|
=|R|-2J\ge0.$$
This permits arbitrary pairing of negative units with distinct positive units. It establishes no local routing or preservation of previous allocations, and the note appropriately limits that claim.The accepted conclusion is that whole-board endpoint invasion cannot raise  $J$  above half the area while the stated selection and anchor hypotheses remain in force. The proof does not cover new black selections outside  $B^*$ , removal of the required occupied anchors, or selection of the two protected bottom white sites. It consequently establishes neither a universal half-area theorem nor a universal improvement of the  $5/6$  bound referred to in the note.
